finding.claim: Unauthenticated POST /hooks/test passes attacker-controlled req.body.callback directly to axios.post, enabling blind SSRF with status-code oracle.

trace.note: pub.post('/hooks/test') registered on pub router with no auth middleware
req.body.callback used as URL for axios.post with no validation
r.status returned to caller, giving internal-host status oracle

finding.guards_checked: None: no scheme allowlist, no host/IP allowlist, no private/loopback/link-local blocking, no DNS pinning, redirects followed by default (axios maxRedirects not disabled). Assumes express body parser mounted upstream (not in this directory).

verdict.guard_found: none. routes.js:19 registers `pub.post("/hooks/test")` with no middleware; the only guard, `requireAdmin` (routes.js:7-10), is attached to `admin` alone (routes.js:12), not `pub`. routes.js:20 passes `req.body.callback` straight to `axios.post` with no scheme, host, IP, or redirect checks.
verdict.reason: The URL comes from the request body at routes.js:20 on a router with no auth (routes.js:19), and nothing validates it before the request is sent, so an unauthenticated caller can make the server send a POST to an arbitrary URL. Two caveats: the status oracle is weaker than claimed, because axios rejects non-2xx by default so routes.js:21 only returns successful statuses and the attacker mostly learns success versus error; and I could not confirm from this directory that `pub` is mounted without an upstream auth middleware, though the code shows no auth on it.

finding.claim: Admin-gated GET /diagnostics/fetch passes req.query.url directly to axios.get, allowing SSRF from an admin session; only the session role check guards it.

trace.note: admin.use(requireAdmin) applies gate to all admin routes

finding.guards_checked: Admin session role gate only (routes.js:7-12). No URL scheme, host, or IP validation; redirects followed by default. Trust in req.session.role depends on session handling outside this directory (not audited).

verdict.reason: Every trace line checks out (routes.js:8 role check, :12 admin.use, :15 axios.get(req.query.url), :16 returns only r.status), and no URL validation exists, but the source is not attacker-controlled by an unauthenticated or low-privilege user: routes.js:8 and :12 limit the route to sessions with role "admin", so the URL comes from an already-privileged admin. Any escalation would depend on session handling, which was not audited, so this is not a standalone SSRF finding from this code.
